issues.description: The study is explicitly retrospective: participants recalled past episodes and the researchers analyzed historical text messages. Calling this a "prospective research design" is conceptually incorrect and overstates the design’s ability to support prediction or temporal inference.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames findings as identifying "real-time" markers and improving imminent risk prediction, but the data are historical and retrospectively labeled. This design can identify retrospective associations only; it cannot establish real-time predictive performance or prospective utility.
issues.quote: Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk.

issues.description: The manuscript gives contradictory definitions of the key exposure window. Attempt episodes are first defined as the one-week period before an attempt, then all episodes are said to be two weeks long, and the time variable is modeled from -14 to 0. This inconsistency makes it unclear what data were actually analyzed and undermines reproducibility.
issues.quote: Episodes included: 1) past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”... The decision to set each episode at two weeks long was made... day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)

issues.description: Attempt episodes are anchored to a concrete event (the attempt), whereas ideation, depressed/high-stress, and typical/positive episodes are arbitrary two-week windows. Comparing slopes across these differently anchored windows is not equivalent and may produce artifactual differences because only attempt episodes are aligned to a salient endpoint.
issues.quote: Episodes included: 1) past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”; 2) two-week episodes of suicide ideation (not resulting in a suicide attempt); 3) two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt); and 4) two-week episode of typical mood

issues.description: The primary outcome conflates enacted attempts with interrupted and aborted attempts, and even includes episodes where no physical attempt occurred. This substantially weakens construct validity because the putative "high-risk" category mixes qualitatively different phenomena and blurs the distinction between ideation, preparation, and attempt.
issues.quote: past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts... (Note that reported ‘suicide attempts’ also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than ‘suicide ideation’ so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions.)

issues.description: The depressed/high-stress comparison group combines depressive episodes with high-stress periods. These are distinct psychological states that may differ linguistically and clinically, so merging them creates a heterogeneous reference category and obscures interpretation.
issues.quote: 3) two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt)

issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently describes the low-risk comparison condition as "positive mood" in some sections but operationalizes it as a "typical mood" episode that is neither particularly positive nor negative. This mismatch obscures what the comparator actually represents.
issues.quote: two-week episode of typical mood (i.e., neither particularly positive nor negative mood and no ideation or attempt)

issues.description: Episode type is the central predictor, yet the manuscript does not report explicit decision rules, thresholds, or any inter-rater/adjudication procedure for classifying episodes. Stating that follow-up questions were asked is not sufficient to evaluate classification validity or reproducibility.
issues.quote: Participants answered additional questions about each reported episode as a way to minimize the risk of misclassification, including episode-specific questions about suicidal thoughts and behaviors, depression/anxiety symptoms, and state mood.

issues.description: The time window was not purely theory-driven; it was also chosen after visually inspecting the data. Selecting the analytic window after examining patterns in the outcome variables introduces researcher degrees of freedom and inflates the risk of capitalizing on chance.
issues.quote: The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced.

issues.description: Only 46% of identified episodes had SMS data, and analyses were ultimately based on 27 of the 33 recruited participants. This level of loss is substantial and may bias results if episodes with recoverable text data differ systematically from those without recoverable data.
issues.quote: A total of 293 episodes were collected across all participants... Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.description: Missing communication data were driven by device encryption, old-phone access, backups, and cloud retrieval problems. These are unlikely to be missing at random and could systematically vary by recency of episode, device type, socioeconomic factors, or texting behavior, threatening validity.
issues.quote: a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data... efforts to collection additional messages outside of their current mobile device were minimally successful.

issues.description: The manuscript suggests mixed models solve the missing-data problem, but mixed models do not eliminate bias from nonrandom missingness. Given the clear device- and time-dependent data loss, this reassurance is overstated.
issues.quote: A mixed-effects method was selected because of its well-established advantages in terms of producing more accurate effect estimates and its ability to handle missing data

issues.description: Including a random intercept for "message" is not appropriate when each message is a single observation. A random effect with one observation per level is effectively unidentifiable/uninformative and suggests model misspecification.
issues.quote: A random by-participant slope for episode type and random intercepts of participant, participant-episode, and message were included as the random effects.

issues.description: The authors intended a maximal random-effects structure but abandoned all random slopes in the time-interaction models because of nonconvergence. This materially changes inferential properties, yet no sensitivity analyses or alternative specifications are reported to assess robustness.
issues.quote: The maximal random effects model appropriate for these data included random intercepts of participant, participant-episode, and message, and random by-participant slopes for episode type, day of episode, and episode type by day. Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.

issues.description: Likelihood-ratio tests and Wald chi-square tests are different inferential procedures, but the manuscript treats them as the same. This makes it unclear what test was actually used and complicates interpretation of the reported omnibus statistics.
issues.quote: Likelihood-ratio (Wald chi-square) tests were performed to compare goodness of fit for models including and excluding the fixed effect of episode type.

issues.description: The manuscript states that β values are standardized effect sizes in log-odds units. Standard GLMM coefficients are not standardized by default, and log-odds coefficients are not themselves standardized effect sizes. This is a statistical reporting error.
issues.quote: Here, β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes.

issues.description: The power analysis uses Cramer's V and chi-square tests as though the primary analyses were simple contingency tests, despite the actual analyses being multilevel mixed models. The stated effective sample size logic ("60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect") is also opaque and not a valid justification for power in this design.
issues.quote: We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes (Cramer’s V=0.29) for chi-square tests of mixed-effects models

issues.description: The power discussion is framed around 30 suicide attempters, but the actual analyzable sample for SMS-based analyses was 27 participants, with only 21 attempts having corresponding SMS data. This further weakens already limited power.
issues.quote: A sample of 33 participants with at least one reported past suicide attempt were recruited... 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants... Among the 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data

issues.description: The manuscript analyzes count variables such as number of messages sent per day as raw continuous outcomes in linear mixed models. These outcomes are typically skewed, bounded at zero, and often overdispersed, making Gaussian LMMs a questionable choice without justification or diagnostics.
issues.quote: For outcome variables that were not proportion scores (e.g., number of messages sent per day), the raw continuous variable was used in a linear mixed-effects model (LMM)

issues.description: The social-engagement outcomes rely on sent/received ratios, but the manuscript does not explain how zeros, undefined ratios, extreme skew, or days with no messages were handled. Without these details, the analyses cannot be evaluated or replicated.
issues.quote: we hypothesized that suicide attempt episodes would demonstrate greater signs of social disengagement (i.e., lower ratio of sent vs. received text messages).

issues.description: The term "numerical factor" is internally contradictory and leaves unclear whether time was treated as continuous or categorical. The manuscript interprets the interaction as a slope, but the coding scheme is not clearly specified, hindering reproducibility and interpretation.
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)

issues.description: Analyzing individual messages rather than episode- or day-level summaries means participants or episodes with very high texting frequency contribute disproportionately to estimation. This may cause results to reflect habits of heavy texters rather than robust within-person episode effects, especially given the huge variability in message counts.
issues.quote: This approach also allowed us to maximize sources of variance by analyzing on the message level rather than only mean values by episode... Across all episodes, 189,478 text messages were collected and analyzed

issues.description: The manuscript reports different p-values for the same omnibus sadness test. The text gives p=.003, whereas Table 2 shows .033. This is a clear internal inconsistency in statistical reporting.
issues.quote: Regarding sentiment, there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.003.

issues.description: The Results section states there was no significant effect for anxiety, but the Discussion claims high-risk periods were associated with greater anxiety. This contradiction misstates the empirical findings.
issues.quote: No significant effects by episode type emerged for more general emotional content (i.e., positive emotion, negative emotion, emotional tone) or other specific emotions/constructs (i.e., anxiety, anger, death). / results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness.

issues.description: The reported means show desire to die increased from pre to post, yet the manuscript states it "decreased slightly." This is a basic error in interpreting descriptive statistics.
issues.quote: desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=1.03, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033.

issues.description: Within-person comparisons do not eliminate confounding by time-varying factors. Episodes likely occurred at different ages, semesters, relationships, treatment phases, phone platforms, and life contexts, but no such covariates were modeled. Thus observed language differences cannot be attributed specifically to suicide risk state.
issues.quote: participants were asked to identify a number of specific events or episodes in the past and the calendar dates during which the episodes took place... A total of 3 to 12 episodes were collected for each participant

issues.description: The sample is predominantly female, White, and college-aged. This substantially limits generalizability to older adults, males, more diverse populations, and clinical settings where suicide risk prediction is most needed.
issues.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

issues.description: Participants with high or imminent current suicide risk were excluded. That means the study does not actually test markers among people currently at highest risk, limiting the relevance of conclusions about identifying imminent suicide risk.
issues.quote: Any participants with intense thoughts of suicide who were determined to be at “high risk” or “imminent risk” for suicidal behavior... were excluded from study participation

issues.description: The study equates first-person singular pronoun use with rumination/negative self-focus. That is a weak and indirect operationalization: pronoun use can reflect many linguistic or conversational factors unrelated to pathological self-focus or rumination.
issues.quote: we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of rumination) was greater prior to suicide attempts

issues.description: Using outgoing vs. incoming message counts as a measure of social engagement, burdensomeness, or belongingness is a poor match to the underlying constructs. Message volume does not directly index perceived burdensomeness or thwarted belongingness.
issues.quote: we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement from and burdensomeness on their social support networks prior to suicide attempts compared to other episodes by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages.

issues.description: The text-analytic approach relies on isolated dictionary words and cannot account for context, negation, sarcasm, or discourse meaning. This weakens inference from LIWC category counts to emotional state.
issues.quote: One weakness of this approach is that examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., “not happy” would count as “positive emotion” because negation is not accounted for)

issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that many analyses were exploratory, but it does not describe a preregistered analysis plan. Given the many outcomes, episode contrasts, and modeling decisions, the absence of preregistration increases researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: Numerous aspects of this research were exploratory by nature.

issues.description: The study ran a large number of tests across many linguistic variables, mean effects, time interactions, and pairwise contrasts, yet explicitly chose not to correct for multiple comparisons. This substantially increases false-positive risk, especially given several marginal p-values near .05.
issues.quote: our analyses involved running a fairly large number of tests... we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction)

issues.description: The manuscript argues that this approach avoids problems with self-report, but the key episode labels that define the within-subject contrasts are entirely based on participants’ retrospective self-report. That contradiction weakens the conceptual framing.
issues.quote: This approach helps avoid the complications inherent to either patient or clinician self-report... participants were asked to identify a number of specific events or episodes in the past

issues.description: Recruitment began with a participant-pool screen requiring endorsement of a past period of sadness with hopelessness. This may select a particular subtype of suicidal history and exclude people whose suicidality was not preceded by that pattern, limiting generalizability.
issues.quote: On the participant pool pretest... participants were asked, “Have you ever had a period of sadness in the past during which you felt hopeless?”

issues.description: Means are reported for intent to die and subjective lethality, but the scale anchors and response options are not provided in the main text. Without scale definitions, these descriptive values are difficult to interpret or compare.
issues.quote: participants reported fairly high intent to kill themselves (M=3.95, SD=0.86) and subjective judgment of the lethality of the suicide method was reasonably high (M=3.38, SD=0.86)

issues.description: Data cleaning is described only at a very high level. The manuscript does not provide enough detail to reproduce preprocessing choices such as handling of emojis, non-English content, attachments, duplicates, group texts, empty messages, or message segmentation artifacts.
issues.quote: participants’ SMS data files were individually cleaned using Python to standardize the encoding of messages and naming of variables across all participants.

issues.description: The manuscript uses LIWC Tone, which it itself describes as a proprietary "non-transparent" variable. Reliance on an opaque measure for inferential results reduces reproducibility and hinders theoretical interpretation.
issues.quote: Other LIWC variables include counts of words (e.g., word count of message, words per sentence) and several proprietary, “non-transparent” variables (e.g., Tone)

issues.description: The study interprets SMS behavior as reflecting communication and social engagement, but other communication channels were collected and then excluded from analysis. For young adults, SMS may represent only a subset of relevant interaction, limiting construct validity for broader social behavior.
issues.quote: Additional forms of personal digital data, including phone call history, Google data (Gmail, Hangouts, and Chrome browser history), Facebook messages, and Twitter messages, were collected for the purposes of future analyses but are not part of the current study.
